title: THE BIBLE’S MESSAGE TO SEXUALLY BROKEN PEOPLE ISN’T “PRETEND IT NEVER HAPPENED”—IT IS REPENTANCE AND REDEMPTION
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S MESSAGE TO SEXUALLY BROKEN PEOPLE ISN’T “PRETEND IT NEVER HAPPENED”—IT IS REPENTANCE AND REDEMPTION

Jesus does not ask you to rename darkness as light, erase your history, or manufacture an innocent past. He does something infinitely greater: He meets you in the truth, calls sin what it is, washes the guilty, receives the repentant, binds the wounded, and gives ruined people a future their past no longer has the authority to write.
There are things people confess out loud.
And then there are things they take to the grave.
The browser history nobody knows about.
The affair that still wakes you up at 2:13 in the morning.
The pornography you promised God you would never watch again.
The relationship you knew crossed boundaries, but loneliness kept whispering, Just one more time.
The body you gave away because you were desperate to feel wanted.
The person you used because desire became stronger than love.
The secret messages.
The hidden fantasies.
The shame after the screen goes dark.
The memory of somebody touching you when you never gave permission.
The childhood wound you still cannot describe without feeling dirty, even though you were the one who was violated.
The marriage damaged by betrayal.
The years of sexual choices you wish you could somehow pull out of your history.
And perhaps the hardest part is Sunday morning.
Because you know how to smile.
You know when to stand.
You know when to sing.
You know how to say, “God is good.”
But somewhere underneath the worship song is a question you are terrified to ask:
If everybody knew the whole story, would they still believe I belonged here?
And beneath even that question is another one.
Does Jesus know everything?
Yes.
Everything.
And that is precisely why what comes next matters.
Because the Bible's message to sexually broken people is not, “Pretend it never happened.”
It is not, “Your choices don't matter.”
It is not, “Your body doesn't matter.”
It is not, “God understands, so keep doing whatever you want.”
But neither is it:
“You are disgusting.”
“You are permanently contaminated.”
“You went too far.”
“You can never become clean again.”
“You will always be what you did.”
The Gospel is far more devastating to sin than that...
and far more merciful to sinners.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth surrounded by sexual immorality and moral confusion, and he refuses to soften the truth. He warns them plainly about unrighteousness and names sexual immorality among the sins incompatible with inheriting the kingdom of God.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in the New Testament.
“And such were some of you.”
Not such are you.
Such were some of you.
Then three enormous words fall like thunder over human shame:
ἀπελούσασθε — apelousasthe — you were washed.
ἡγιάσθητε — hēgiasthēte — you were sanctified, made holy, set apart.
ἐδικαιώθητε — edikaiōthēte — you were justified, declared righteous.
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11
Do not rush past that.
Paul does not say they imagined their past away.
He does not say their sins were insignificant.
He does not tell them to pretend Corinth never happened.
He says something far more astonishing.
Christ happened.
There is a difference.
Christian redemption does not require historical amnesia.
You may remember what happened.
You may remember what you did.
You may remember who you became.
You may even carry consequences that forgiveness does not instantly erase.
But the Gospel declares that your past does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is why Christianity can look directly at sexual sin without blinking.
We do not need to pretend sin is harmless in order to prove that God is loving.
The cross proves something much greater.
Sin was serious enough that Christ died.
Grace was powerful enough that He willingly did.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to solve shame by changing vocabulary.
You called bondage “freedom.”
You called lust “just being human.”
You called adultery “finally finding happiness.”
You called pornography “stress relief.”
You called compromise “love.”
You called what God told you to leave “complicated.”
But changing the label never healed the wound.
Jesus does not redeem the imaginary person you pretend to be.
He redeems the sinner who finally comes into the light.
That is why biblical repentance is beautiful.
The New Testament repeatedly uses the language of μετάνοια — metanoia — repentance, a turning of mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is not making yourself clean enough for Jesus.
You cannot.
It is not hating yourself until God believes you are sorry.
Self-hatred is not the Gospel.
Repentance is the sinner finally dropping the defense.
No more excuses.
No more hiding.
No more negotiating with what is destroying you.
No more demanding that God call holy what He calls sin.
You turn toward Christ.
You confess.
You surrender.
And you discover that the Savior standing before the repentant sinner is not holding a stone.
He is holding scars.
There is something else that must be said, because careless religious language has wounded people God never accused.
Not every sexually broken person is broken because of sexual sin they chose.
Some were sinned against.
If somebody abused you, assaulted you, exploited you, groomed you, coerced you, manipulated you, or violated you, their sin does not become your guilt.
You do not need to repent for being victimized.
You are not morally contaminated because another person committed evil against you.
What happened matters.
Justice matters.
Truth matters.
Healing matters.
And Jesus is not standing over the wounded asking why they were wounded.
Scripture shows Him drawing near to the crushed and brokenhearted.
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.”
—Psalm 34:18

There may be wounds requiring patient healing. There may be trauma that needs wise pastoral care and qualified professional help. There may be crimes that need to be reported to appropriate authorities. Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good, abandoning justice, or placing yourself back within reach of an abuser.
Jesus is not glorified by protecting darkness.
He is glorified by truth.
And whether your story is primarily the story of sins you committed, sins committed against you, or a painfully tangled mixture of both, the invitation of Christ remains astonishing:
Come into the light.
Because shame says, Hide.
Jesus says, Come.
Shame says, If people knew, you would be finished.
Jesus says, I already know.
Shame says, This is who you are.
The Gospel says, Such were some of you.
Perhaps that sentence is why you were meant to read this today.
Such were some of you.
The Bible never says, “Such never happened to you.”
It says something better.
Your history may describe where you have been.
It does not get the final word on who you become in Christ.
David committed adultery and arranged the death of Uriah. When Nathan confronted him, David did not receive permission to rename his rebellion. He was brought to confession.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
—2 Samuel 12:13
Psalm 51 gives us the cry of a man who understood that grace is not pretending.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
—Psalm 51:10
The Hebrew plea is breathtaking:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
David does not merely ask God to improve his public image.
He asks God for cleansing at the center of who he is.
That is repentance.
And that is why cheap grace cannot save anyone from bondage.
If the message were merely, “God forgives you, so don't worry about what you're doing,” there would be no rescue in it.
Imagine telling a drowning person:
“The water loves you exactly where you are.”
No.
Love reaches into the water.
Love pulls you toward life.
Grace does not merely comfort us inside slavery.
Grace breaks chains.
Jesus said:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
—John 8:36
Free indeed.
Not free to polish the chains.
Not free to decorate the prison.
Not free to rename captivity.
Free.
Maybe you have prayed after falling into the same sexual sin so many times that even your own apology sounds fake to you.
“God, forgive me.”
Again.
Then again.
Then again.
And eventually the enemy begins preaching his own sermon:
Look at you.
You will never change.
You don't really love God.
Why bother coming back?
Listen carefully.
The fact that repeated sin is serious does not mean repeated return to Christ is pointless.
You do not defeat sin by running away from the only One who can save you from it.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it.
Cut off what feeds it.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Stop arranging private access to the thing you publicly claim you want freedom from.
If an app keeps becoming a doorway, close the doorway.
If a conversation keeps becoming seduction, end the conversation.
If secrecy keeps feeding bondage, break secrecy with trustworthy, mature believers.
Jesus used radical language about removing occasions of sin because holiness is not a hobby.
But hear this carefully:
Your discipline does not purchase God's mercy.
Jesus purchased your redemption.
You fight from grace, not for the right to receive grace.
That difference changes everything.
Because at the center of Christianity is not a sexually flawless person congratulating himself for being better than everybody else.
At the center is a crucified Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
The sinless One.
The Lamb of God.
The One who bore sin He never committed so sinners could receive righteousness they could never earn.
At the cross, God does not pretend sin never happened.
He judges sin.
At the cross, God does not pretend sinners are innocent because their behavior does not matter.
Christ bears judgment.
At the cross, mercy does not defeat justice by ignoring it.
Mercy comes through the sacrifice of Jesus.
And at the empty tomb, we discover that scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Death itself does not get the final chapter.
This is why there is no Christian redemption without Jesus Christ.
Therapy may help you understand patterns.
Accountability may help you break secrecy.
Boundaries may protect you.
Wise counseling may help heal wounds.
Community may carry you when you are weak.
These can be profound gifts of God's common and providential grace.
But none of them can become your Savior.
Only Jesus reconciles sinners to God.
Only Christ bore our sins.
Only Christ rose from the dead.
Only Christ can say to the guilty who trust Him that condemnation no longer owns their future.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction says, This must change. Come back to God.
Condemnation says, You can never come back.
Learn the difference.
One leads you toward the Father.
The other makes you hide from Him.
Somebody needs to stop confusing shame with holiness.
Feeling filthy forever is not evidence that you have adequately respected the seriousness of your sin.
If Christ has forgiven you, insisting that your guilt is stronger than His cross is not humility.
Bring your sin to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Then get up and walk with Him.
Perhaps slowly.
Perhaps with tears.
Perhaps with accountability.

Perhaps with trembling hands deleting numbers, ending relationships, installing safeguards, confessing secrets, seeking counseling, rebuilding a marriage, learning healthy intimacy, grieving what happened to you, or finally telling somebody trustworthy what you have carried alone for years.
But walk.
One obedient step after another.
Because sanctification often looks less like one cinematic moment and more like a thousand quiet decisions to keep saying yes to Jesus.
And if you fall?
Do not make peace with the ground.
Get up.
Run toward Christ.
Confess honestly.
Learn what opened the door.
Strengthen the boundary.
Receive help.
Keep walking.
The goal is not to become somebody who can brag, “I fixed myself.”
The goal is to become somebody whose life says:
“Look what Jesus Christ can redeem.”
That is why the words “such were some of you” should shake the Church.
There should be people sitting in our congregations whose former lives would scandalize us if we knew every detail.
Former adulterers.
Former porn addicts.
Former prostitutes.
Former exploiters.
Formerly promiscuous men and women.
People whose histories are complicated.
People whose scars remain.
People whose families were shattered.
People who once believed they were beyond saving.
And now?
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not because the Church lowered God's standard.
Because Jesus paid the sinner's debt.
Not because sin became less sinful.
Because grace proved greater than their rebellion.
This is the kind of Church sexually broken people need.
Not a Church afraid to call sin sin.
And not a Church addicted to making sinners feel permanently unclean.
Truth without grace crushes.
Grace without truth deceives.
Jesus Christ brings truth and grace together.
Maybe this article is not primarily about “those people.”
Maybe it is about you.
The secret you have protected while reading every paragraph.
The memory that made your stomach tighten.
The name that came into your mind.
The habit you immediately tried to justify.
The wound you still blame yourself for.
The confession you know you need to make.
The surrender you have postponed.
You do not have to tell the internet every detail of your story.
Wisdom matters.
Privacy matters.
But you do need to stop lying to God.
And perhaps tonight the most spiritual thing you can do is close the door, put the phone down, kneel somewhere nobody can applaud you, and finally tell Jesus the truth.
“Lord, this is what happened.”
“Lord, this is what I did.”
“Lord, this is what was done to me.”
“Lord, this is what I keep returning to.”
“Lord, I cannot free myself.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is no magic in the wording.
The power is not in an emotional formula.
The power is in Christ.
Turn to Him.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details.
And if Christ has already begun rewriting a chapter you once thought could never be redeemed, tell somebody below:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed to survive tonight.
And if you know somebody quietly drowning beneath sexual shame, send this to them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose them.
Send it privately if wisdom requires it.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has wandered.
Invite the believer growing cold.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Because the Gospel was never meant to remain trapped inside people who have already heard it.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
God does not owe us blessings because we clicked a button.
Christian giving is worship when it flows freely from a heart that belongs to Christ: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
People are.
Souls matter more than sales.
If God has blessed you through this ministry, prayerfully consider helping us keep going.
Send it personally to the person whose name will not leave your heart.
Comment so another struggling believer sees they are not the only person fighting.
Follow because none of us outgrow our need for Scripture.
And above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot wash you.
A comment cannot justify you.
A book cannot redeem you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Jesus Christ can.
Maybe your story really is scandalous.
Maybe some of it was your fault.
Maybe some of it absolutely was not.
Maybe you carry both repentance and wounds.
Maybe you have consequences you cannot reverse.
Maybe people still remember who you used to be.
Maybe you remember too.
But if you belong to Christ, there are three words the enemy desperately hopes you never learn to say with confidence:
“Such. Were. Some.”
Were.
There is an entire Gospel hiding inside that tense.
You were not saved because the scandal never happened.
You were saved because Jesus entered the story.
And when Jesus enters a surrendered story, He does not need to erase yesterday to prove that yesterday no longer owns tomorrow.
Your darkest chapter may remain part of your testimony—but it does not get to hold the pen when Jesus Christ has taken hold of your life.
